profile.reading:
Sabey Data Centers operates SDC Columbia, a data center campus at 4405 Grant Road in East Wenatchee, Douglas County, Washington, in the Columbia River region. Sabey traces its roots to 1972, when Dave Sabey founded Sabey Corporation as a Pacific Northwest commercial real estate developer; the company entered the data center business almost by accident during the dot-com collapse, when a vacated tenant building in Seattle became SDC Seattle Building 5. Sabey Data Centers itself was formally established in 2010 as a joint venture between Sabey Corporation and institutional investor National Real Estate Advisors, a structure confirmed on both the operator's own site and independently by Wikipedia. As of 2026 Sabey operates seven data center campuses nationally, together totaling more than 3.5 million square feet and, per Wikipedia's most recent figure, nearly 400 MW of capacity; Tim Mirick became Sabey's president effective January 1, 2025, succeeding Rob Rockwood.

Per the operator's own SDC Columbia page, the East Wenatchee campus is marketed on renewable hydroelectric power priced at 5 cents per kilowatt-hour, drawn from the Columbia River hydroelectric system that also supplies neighboring Quincy, Washington's data center cluster. The campus comprises three completed buildings plus a fourth under construction, totaling roughly 70 MW of capacity campus-wide, a figure the operator does not break out per individual building. Aggregator Baxtel separately reports an additional 9 MW of Tier III-standard critical power expected at the campus from Q4 2026, a forward-looking figure not yet delivered as of this writing and not applied as confirmed capacity to any building here.

This specific building, Intergate Columbia D, is listed by aggregator DatacenterHawk at the same 4405 Grant Road street address as the general campus listing and as neighboring Building B; no distinct street number specific to Building D has been located in sourcing to date, consistent with a shared-campus-address pattern also seen elsewhere in this operator's portfolio.
profile.capacity_note: not published at the building level. Campus wide total is 70 MW (operator figure), not applied to this individual building. Baxtel separately notes 9 MW of additional Tier III capacity expected campus wide from Q4 2026, a future figure not applied to critical_it_mw.

reading.body:
Intergate Columbia D sits on the SDC Columbia campus in East Wenatchee, Washington, a four-building complex in Douglas County's Columbia River hydroelectric region. The operator publishes only a campus-wide capacity of 70 MW across all buildings without breaking out individual building figures. Building D is currently under construction and no building-level power allocation has been published. The campus qualifies to host HIPAA and HITECH regulated workloads, PCI DSS payment processing, and ISO 27001 security-certified operations. A planned additional 9 MW of Tier III critical power is expected campus-wide from Q4 2026 but is not yet operational.

At the published 70 MW campus total, this facility ranks third by capacity among the two facilities in Washington state that publish power figures, though it sits among 46 mapped data center locations statewide. The state's total published capacity is 60 MW, making SDC Columbia's 70 MW a landmark figure in Washington data center infrastructure, but this represents only a campus total unavailable for per-building allocation. The hydroelectric power contract at 5 cents per kilowatt-hour indicates cost positioning for long-duration workloads rather than peak-density AI training racks.

Because the operator does not publish building-level capacity, the computational density of Intergate Columbia D cannot be determined from published sources. A 70 MW campus allocation across four buildings suggests roughly 17.5 MW per building as a division, which at 40 kW per rack is approximately 440 racks per building as an assumption, but this assumes even distribution and may misallocate to construction phases. Until building-specific capacity is published, the site's relevance to AI scaling decisions turns on the campus's hydroelectric cost and grid reliability rather than absolute scale.
